extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato and classical political/philosophical literature; readers interested in education, censorship, and aesthetics in the Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and prescriptions from Plato's Republic (as discussed in the commentary) about which stories, styles, music, arts, and educational practices are appropriate for citizens (especially guardian youth) in the ideal State. Covers censorship, pedagogy, artistic form, music/metre, physical training, and selection of office-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of nursery tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ought not to learn stories which are untrue or immoral; nursery tales must be censored, banishing some and keeping others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper tales: Homer and Hesiod's accounts (Uranus and Saturn stories, gods inciting wrongs, e.g. Athene and Zeus inciting Pandarus), narratives that encourage children to beat their fathers or imitate divine wrongdoing. The young are impressible and should not be taught what they will later have to unlearn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the gods — God as author of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God must be represented as he is: not as the author of evil but of good only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permit poets to depict gods as stewards of both good and evil, or as causing men to sin or suffer for arbitrary purposes. Prohibits tales that make God responsible for evil deeds (e.g., attributing Niobe's sufferings, Trojan war, or Pandarus' treaty-breaking to God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the gods — immutability and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: God is unchangeable and absolutely true; he does not change form or deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetic motifs of gods assuming disguises or deceptive forms (e.g., gods prowling at night in strange disguises). Argues that gods have no need for lying or deception; portrayals that suggest otherwise are 'blasphemous nonsense' to be suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on use of falsehood (noble lie) — reserved to rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsehoods or fictions may be used as medicines for the populace, but their use must be strictly limited to the rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato allows 'economies' or controlled fictions when required for moral effect, but insists such dangerous weapons should be employed only by rulers and for great objects; common people must not be permitted to tell lies to the rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purging tales that produce fear or cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: Expunge passages that foster fear of death or the underworld; soldiers and guardians must not be taught discouraging or terror-inducing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban Homeric depictions of Cocytus, Styx, ghosts, and tartarean horrors and sentiments like Achilles' preference for servitude over rulership of the dead. Such tales are not proper food for soldiers and undermine courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on portraying gods or heroes as weak in ways that encourage imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow portrayals of gods or heroes exhibiting weakness, excessive lamentation, or immoral conduct that the young might imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid scenes like the goddesses' lamentations, Zeus' regrets, Hephaestus' clumsy humiliation, or Achilles' tears and excesses. These depictions risk modeling weakness, lamentation, or vice for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and self-control as central educational goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth must be taught temperance — self-control and obedience to authority — and not exposed to praise of intemperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject Homeric language that praises eating, drinking, rapturous love, or indulgence. Temperance should be instilled so citizens march 'in silent awe of their leaders' and avoid excessive laughter as 'violent delights' lead to violent re-actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit representation/praise of bribery, meanness, cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives that normalize bribery, greed, meanness, or cruelty must be excluded because they encourage immorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples to ban: lines that imply 'gifts persuade the gods' or episodes where heroes take gifts (Achilles taking gifts from Agamemnon), require ransom (Hector), drag corpses, or commit cruelty—such portrayals are unworthy and likely to be imitated by youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching sequence: imagination before reason (falsehood first, truth afterwards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children must be taught through imagination initially and through reason later; early instruction can legitimately use fictions to prepare the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato affirms a staged development: youth learn via stories and imaginative forms because their minds develop gradually; later they can be instructed in truths once reason matures. The line between allowable economy and unacceptable falsehood is drawn by moral effect and necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative style preference: descriptive over imitative/dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer descriptive (narrator-led) style rather than dramatic imitation; guardians should avoid being imitators/actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three styles: simple (description), imitative (dramatic), and mixed. Guardians, who 'cannot play many parts,' should avoid dramatic imitation because the mask can become the face; they should employ descriptive style with minimal imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on imitating base or inferior characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors/poets must not represent or imitate inferior, base, or corrupt characters (slaves, bullies, cowards, drunkards, madmen, craftsmen, animals, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of forbidden impersonations: playing women in labour or love, slaves, bullies, cowards, drunkards, madmen, blacksmiths, neighing horses, bellowing bulls, roaring rivers, raging seas. Imitating such roles corrupts the actor and the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of simplicity in style, metre, and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must conform to subject and metre to style; simplicity and harmony should characterize poetry and music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmony and metre should be simple and suitable to occasion; the 'simplicity and harmony of the soul' should be reflected in artistic forms. Damon is cited for arranging martial and lyrical measures; overall motto: conform style to subject and keep forms simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical selection: forbid mixed/convivial Lydian/Ionian strains; permit Dorian and Phrygian
rubrics_metrics.description: Ban mixed Lydian and Ionian harmonies associated with lamentation or conviviality; permit Dorian (war) and Phrygian (peace/religious) modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Dorian expresses courage, Phrygian obedience/instruction/religious feeling. Also ban complex many-stringed instruments (especially the flute) that support decadent harmonies; allow lyre and harp in town and Pan's-pipe in fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict complex instruments and instrumental variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject many-stringed, variously-shaped instruments and the flute because they support corrupting harmonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted instruments: lyre and harp in the town, Pan's-pipe in the fields. The flute and excessively complex instruments are associated with morally harmful musical forms and should be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purging metres: prefer specific simple rhythms
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter must be simple and appropriate; certain rhythmic ratios and feet have characteristic moral/affective effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned ratios: 3/2, 2/2, 2/1; Damon arranges martial measures, dactylic, trochaic, and iambic rhythms aligning quantity to syllables. The general principle is that metre should fit style and support simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual arts must conform to simplicity and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture and painting must avoid meanness or deformity and conform to the law of simplicity to preserve citizens' taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists who violate simplicity and produce deformity must not be allowed to work in the city because such images 'poison and corrupt' the souls of guardians who must grow up amid health and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as formative: early musical education shapes the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is the chief educator of the soul and imparts the sense of beauty and deformity; early unconscious musical training prepares the soul for reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must first teach the elements (letters/virtue elements) separately and then combinations; music reaches the innermost soul and predisposes the mind to welcome reason when it arrives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastics and diet suited to guardians' role
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians require a simpler kind of gymnastics and diet appropriate to warrior habits; avoid strong drink and excessive palaestra practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warrior athletes should be 'wide-awake dogs' inured to changes of food and climate; Homeric model: feed heroes on roast meat only, avoid fish, boiled meats, sweet sauces, Sicilian cookery, and culinary luxuries tied to decadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice for the State: limited, public-minded medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine should not preserve useless, pampered lives; public medicine should adopt a 'kill or cure' attitude and not indulge treatment of luxury-caused ailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asclepius' practice preferred simple cures for honest diseases; doctors should not treat the intemperate for profit, nor create a class of people who leisurely rely on medical attention. Excessive care of health is inconsistent with ordinary occupation and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for judges: innocence plus observational experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal judge should be of a mature age, have had an innocent youth, and acquire insight into vice by observing it in others rather than by practising it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicians should have bodily experience of disease; judges should not gain experience through committing crimes (criminal-turned-detective is overly suspicious). Vice can be known of virtue, but cannot know virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating State and individual in moral evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish collective/political action from individual ethics; the good man and good citizen only coincide in the perfect State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational and legislative measures cannot simply impose perfection from without; moral formation requires internal education. This is a criterion for judging policies or art that elevate politics into ethics or lower ethics to politics.
